Glitchlock · reversibility bench

Scramble it,
get it back exactly.

Glitchlock wrecks a video under a key and unwinds it later from a 1 KB manifest. This page does not ask you to believe that. It carries the actual bitstreams, hashes them in your browser, and re-implements the cipher in JavaScript to check it against the real locked file.

Signal path

Three files, one round trip

A 3-second clip encoded to an MPEG-2 elementary stream, locked with a key, then unlocked with the same key. The digests below are computed in your browser, right now, from the actual bitstreams embedded in this page — not copied from a build log.

Comparing digests… hashing 1.1 MB of embedded bitstream

The videos are re-encoded to H.264 so a browser can play them — that copy is illustration. The proof is the digest of the MPEG-2 elementary stream itself, which is the file glitchlock actually operates on.

Independent check

The same maths, written twice

Matching hashes prove the tool undoes itself. They do not prove the tool does what it claims. So this page contains a second, independent implementation of the cipher — written in JavaScript, running in your browser — fed the real motion vectors exported from the carrier. It derives its own keystream with HMAC-SHA256, applies its own substitution and permutation, and compares the result against the motion vectors actually found inside locked.mpg.

·JavaScript lock output matches the real locked bitstream — every vector componentwaiting
·JavaScript unlock recovers the carrier's vectors — exactlywaiting
·Every locked value stays inside its codec domain — nothing clippedwaiting
·A permutation preserves the frame's value multiset — nothing invented or lostwaiting
·The wrong key fails to recover — the key is load-bearingwaiting
Using the key this file was locked with.

Change a single hex digit and the agreement collapses. That is the whole security claim in one control: without the exact key, the plan is a different plan, and the vectors land somewhere else.

Mechanism

Why it can invert at all

A decoded motion vector is sign-extended to a fixed bit width derived from the frame's f_code. Write a value past the end of that width and the decoder does not clamp it and does not reject it — it wraps it. A wrapping field is a cyclic group, and modular arithmetic on a cyclic group is exactly invertible. That single measured property is what the whole tool stands on.

Measured against FFglitch 0.10.2 at f_code = 1: values written into a real frame, then read back out. Each codec follows its own modulus and only its own.
Value writtenMPEG-2 reads backMPEG-4 reads backVerdict
—

The two-bit difference that bites

MPEG-2 sign-extends to f_code + 4 bits; MPEG-4 and H.263 use f_code + 5. A real MPEG-4 file legitimately holds the vector 17 at f_code 1. Assume the MPEG-2 width and it silently becomes -15, permanently. This was a live bug during development, caught by the round-trip suite, and it is now a named regression test.

Permutation has to respect domains

Vectors are shuffled only between slots with an identical domain. Move a value from an f_code 5 frame into an f_code 1 slot and it no longer fits, so the codec wraps it and the information is gone. Bucketing by domain is not tidiness; it is correctness.

Negative result

What had to be thrown out

FFedit will happily let you edit DCT coefficients, and they make the prettiest mess of all. They are also not reversible, so glitchlock refuses them by name rather than offering them with a warning. This is the measurement that settled it.

// wrote scrambled DC values, re-exported, compared
STRUCTURE CHANGED  254 -> 223
STRUCTURE CHANGED  279 -> 228
STRUCTURE CHANGED  230 -> 212
STRUCTURE CHANGED  280 -> 272
   ... 94 of 100 frames affected

// what the decoder said
ac-tex damaged at 16 6
invalid cbp -1 at 7 3
slice mismatch
mb incr damaged

The slot count itself moved

DC and AC coefficients are variable-length coded, so changing a value changes how many bits it occupies and shifts everything after it. The re-exported payload came back with a different number of slots than the one written. A manifest can repair a wrong value; nothing can repair a payload that has changed shape. q_dc, q_dct, mv_delta and mb are all refused.

Repairs: the honesty valve

        
After locking, glitchlock reads its own output back and records anything the encoder did
        not reproduce as a literal original value in the manifest. On mv and
        qscale that list comes back empty every time — which is the result you
        want, and is asserted by the test suite rather than assumed. Then lock unlocks
        its own output and compares digests before writing a manifest at all. A lock that cannot be
        proven reversible is never shipped.

      

    

  


  

    
Glitchlock · reversible,
    keyed bitstream scrambling built on FFglitch 0.10.2.
    Source: github.com/armeehn/glitchlock. 259 tests pass from a clean clone,
    including byte-exact round trips on MPEG-2, MPEG-4, H.264, HEVC and MP2.

    
This is a keyed reversible scrambler, not confidentiality. The ciphertext is a playable
    video and leaks its own content — the residual picture survives. For secrecy, encrypt the
    file with a real AEAD tool instead.

    
Set in IBM Plex (SIL Open Font License). FFglitch is GPL and is invoked as an external
